title: Researchers found a way to hijack devices through Zoom screen sharing
gist: Researchers at A Security used publicly available AI models and fewer than 20 prompts to find zero-click vulnerabilities in Zoom's screen-sharing annotation protocol that allowed full device takeover across every OS Zoom supports — work they estimate would previously have taken five people six months.

insights.claim: A Security found the Zoom vulnerabilities in early June using publicly available AI models and fewer than 20 prompts, compressing what the firm estimates was previously a five-person, six-month effort.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: If elite zero-day discovery drops from ~30 person-months to a single afternoon of prompting, the supply of exploitable bugs in closed-source enterprise software rises sharply — bullish for security spend, bearish for anyone whose moat is obscurity.
insights.quote: Before it would have taken a team of five people maybe six months with a lot of refining and iteration to find this. Now people can reach the same results with under 20 prompts.
insights.locator: What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous

insights.claim: The critical shift is democratization rather than capability — the barrier to entry for finding device-takeover bugs is dropping rapidly because the tooling is publicly available, not restricted to state actors.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Threat models built around a small number of well-resourced adversaries need rewriting; the relevant population of capable attackers is now orders of magnitude larger.
insights.quote: the democratization of these capabilities—the barrier to entry is dropping rapidly
insights.locator: What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous

insights.claim: AI bug-hunting systems replicate human researcher heuristics, deliberately targeting convoluted and obscure functions where overlooked vulnerabilities cluster — meaning the automation inherits and scales proven prioritization strategy, not just brute force.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Predicts where the next wave of AI-found bugs will land: esoteric, complex, rarely reviewed features in proprietary software — a triage map for defenders and for shorting exposure.
insights.quote: they have been trained that convoluted and obscure functions often contain overlooked vulnerabilities
insights.locator: The vulnerabilities were specifically in the protocol

insights.claim: Closed-source proprietary software is structurally more exposed to this shift than open source because internal code review lacks the benefit of public, open scrutiny on esoteric features.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A contrarian read on the usual security-through-obscurity argument: AI-assisted auditing may invert the historic open-source vulnerability disadvantage.
insights.quote: An established company like Zoom presumably does extensive code review and vetting on all components and functions, but without the benefit of public, open review, esoteric yet complex features like annotation are more likely to contain mistakes.
insights.locator: This is particularly true with proprietary, closed-source software.

insights.claim: The flaws sat in the protocol handling real-time annotation during screen sharing, and affected every operating system Zoom supports — Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS and Android — making platform diversity no defense.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Cross-platform protocol bugs defeat the usual mitigation of mixed fleets; enterprises assuming Mac or Linux endpoints reduce risk were wrong here.
insights.quote: which affected devices running all operating systems that Zoom supports—Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android
insights.locator: Zoom issued a security advisory on Tuesday

insights.claim: Both participants and hosts of any call involving screen sharing were exposed to a silent attack requiring no victim interaction and giving no indication it was occurring.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Zero-click, zero-indicator means no user-training mitigation and no forensic breadcrumb — detection has to be network- or endpoint-side.
insights.quote: Anyone on a call that involved screen sharing, whether participants or the host, would have been vulnerable to a silent attack that could be carried out with no indication and no interaction from the victim.
insights.locator: As AI models gain advanced capabilities

insights.claim: Zoom shipped both server-side and client-side fixes alongside a Tuesday security advisory, but declined to respond to multiple WIRED requests for comment on the findings.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Dual-sided patching means partial remediation until every client updates; the communications silence is itself a signal about disclosure posture.
insights.quote: The bugs are now patched, with Zoom issuing both server and client-side fixes
insights.locator: Zoom did not respond to multiple requests for comment

insights.claim: Zoom is a uniquely valuable target because joining a call is itself an act of trust, and the platform's use for webinars and semipublic events means attackers can reach targets who have their guard down.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Semipublic meeting platforms are an underpriced initial-access vector — relevant to any enterprise that runs open webinars or external calls.
insights.quote: And Zoom is an important type of target because people assume trust when using it. They don’t see it as a threat.
insights.locator: What is interesting for us and what we believe is dangerous

insights.claim: A Security frames the worst case as full enterprise compromise: take control of one employee's computer and credentials during a call, then move laterally through the organization.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Reclassifies video conferencing from productivity tool to critical attack surface, which should push it up the patch-priority and vendor-risk list.
insights.quote: The worst-case scenario is that we can take over an enterprise just by having this vulnerability in our hands.
insights.locator: If you just get on a Zoom with us, we can take over your device,

insights.claim: The researchers conducted their own disclosure interview on Microsoft Teams rather than Zoom, an implicit operational-security judgment by the people who best understood the exposure.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Insider behavior is often the sharpest signal about residual risk — worth noting when weighing vendor assurances that a bug is fully remediated.
insights.quote: (It was, incidentally, hosted on Microsoft Teams.)
insights.locator: If you just get on a Zoom with us

insights.claim: The security industry's long-running cat-and-mouse dynamic has become an all-out race as AI bug hunting proliferates, implying defensive tooling must adopt the same automation or fall permanently behind.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Frames the investable thesis: automated offensive research forces automated defensive research, expanding the addressable market for AI-native security vendors on both sides.
insights.quote: Practitioners often call security a “cat-and-mouse game,” but as AI bug hunting proliferates, this delicate dance has become an all-out race.
